text: The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers. Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available". If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on. The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence: The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model. The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account. There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas , whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms. Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change". The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory: The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it. Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner. The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind. Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team. Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack. So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms. The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly. Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves. A few edge cases are documented: Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly. The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices. Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent: Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically. The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use. Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce. If you build an agent product on Workspace: If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp , will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive. If you're a Workspace admin: the new controls are under Admin console → Security → API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents. If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.
